name: Summit Block — North Face Direct Finish (variation)

text.approach: From the Hoh Rain Forest trailhead, follow the Hoh River Trail east through old-growth rainforest along the Hoh River. Established camps/toilets appear at roughly 5-Mile Island, the Olympus Guard Station (~9 mi, near the High Hoh Bridge), Lewis Meadow (~11 mi, 1,000 ft — the usual overnight on a 2-day approach, gravel bars/bear wire/privy), and Elk Lake (~15.5 mi) before the trail climbs steeply through forest to Glacier Meadows (17.3–17.4 mi, ~4,300 ft, community bear-wire, standard high camp). Watch for a washed-out, ladder-assisted cliffside stretch around mile 16 (rungs have been reported missing/broken in recent seasons), fallen-log stream crossings, and early-season steep snow on the lower trail calling for an axe; travel above Elk Lake carries avalanche exposure outside summer. Water is frequent the whole way. From Glacier Meadows a way-path climbs ~0.8 mi to the crest of the Blue Glacier's lateral moraine, then follows the moraine ~0.2 mi (steep, loose — some parties fix a short line) before dropping onto the ice; rope up here, crevasse-rescue kit mandatory. Cross the flat lower glacier and climb moderate snow, threading rock islands right of the main icefall before swinging back left below the massif, to Snow Dome (~6,600–6,800 ft), a common high camp ~1,000 ft below the summit. text.overview: The most direct of the three summit-block finishes: a single ~80-ft pitch straight up the north face on mostly solid rock. It's the cleanest line on the pinnacle and conveniently shares ground with the north-side rappel descent.
text.descent: The North Face Direct Finish climbs straight up the ~80 ft north face on generally solid rock (5.4, one pitch) rather than the standard east-face ramp system — enough parties end up on this exact line that a semi-permanent rap anchor has built up at the top: a boulder/horn rigged with slings, a rap ring, and a quick link (inspect and back up any fixed tat, it is not agency-maintained). text.approach: No maintained trail reaches the north face. Parties generally leave the West Ridge boot path or approach cross-country from the Anderson Creek drainage / FR 6220 area, bushwhacking through steep second-growth and old-growth timber to gain the base of the wall; expect substantial off-trail forest travel and real route-finding difficulty.

text.overview: A difficult, multi-pitch technical alpine rock climb up Mount Persis's sheer north face, established by prolific North Cascades first-ascentionist Bryan Burdo.

text.approach: Take the Dingford Creek trail about 2.2 miles to its crossing of Goat Creek (about 2,600 ft). Leave the trail, cross the valley southward, and enter the basin that holds Price Lake.

text.approach: From I-5 exit 208 head east 4 miles on Highway 530 to Arlington, then continue east on SR 530 for 28 miles to Darrington. At the four-way intersection in town turn right onto the Mountain Loop Highway and follow paved then graveled road for roughly 12.5-14 miles to a prominent Mount Pugh sign, where FR 2095 branches off on the left. FR 2095 is narrow, one-lane and unpaved; drive it about 1.5 miles to the signed trailhead on the right at the second switchback, elevation 1,900-1,920 ft. Parking is limited, there are no facilities, and the road is reportedly narrow enough that potholes are unavoidable. From the car, Mt Pugh Trail #644 climbs steadily through mature forest with a few stream crossings for about 1.5 miles to Lake Metan (Metam) at roughly 3,180-3,260 ft — this is the last reliable water on the route, so tank up here. The trail rounds the north side of the lake and then switchbacks hard up steep forested slopes, breaking out into an open boulder-strewn basin at around 4,900 ft before topping out at Stujack Pass, 5,700-5,750 ft, at about 4.5 miles. Above the pass the character changes completely: the path climbs leftward out of the notch on heather, contours the east side of the ridge, crosses the head of a small permanent snowfield and takes to the crest on chipped, blasted ledges. text.overview: A short, easy trad rock pitch (5.0) on one of several small crags directly above the Mt Pugh Trail between Stujack Pass and the summit — a minor, lightly-documented technical option rather than the way most parties climb the peak.
text.descent: There is nothing to descend from the slab itself beyond the short class 3 downclimb to the right. The real descent is the whole Northwest Ridge scramble in reverse, and that is where accidents happen on this mountain. waypoints.name: Mount Pugh Trailhead, FR 2095 second switchback
waypoints.directions: From I-5 exit 208, head east 4 miles on Highway 530 to Arlington, then continue east on SR 530 another 28 miles to Darrington. At the four-way intersection in town turn right onto the Mountain Loop Highway and follow it, paved and then graveled, for roughly 12.5 to 14 miles to a prominent Mount Pugh sign where FR 2095 branches off on the left. FR 2095 is narrow, one-lane and unpaved, and narrow enough that the potholes are unavoidable; drive it about 1.5 miles to the signed trailhead on the right at the second switchback, around 1,900 ft. Parking is limited and there are no facilities.

waypoints.name: Lake Metan (Metam) — last reliable water
waypoints.directions: Follow Mt. Pugh Trail #644 about 1.5 miles up through mature forest, with a few stream crossings, to Lake Metan near 3,200 ft. Fill up here; there is no reliable water higher on the mountain.

waypoints.name: Stujack Pass — decision point, scramble begins, Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary
waypoints.directions: Round the north side of the lake, then switchback hard up steep forested slopes, breaking out into an open boulder-strewn basin near 4,900 ft, and continue up to the notch of Stujack Pass at about 5,700 ft, where the maintained trail ends.

text.approach: Reached from the summit of either Mount Rahm (via the Standard Route/Glacier or South Side) or Mount Custer (via its South Ridge), not from a trailhead directly.

text.overview: A high, mostly Class 2/3 ridge-crest traverse directly connecting the summits of Mount Rahm and Mount Custer, with one short Class 4 gully bypassing an unclimbable arête near Custer's summit block.
text.descent: Parties doing this traverse essentially never reverse it. From Custer's summit, descend the South Ridge route back toward Ouzel Lake or the Depot Creek-Silver Lake saddle camp; from Rahm's summit, descend the South Side route's gully system back to camp.

text.approach: Reached from the closed Westside Road beyond the Dry Creek gate on a long walk in of about 12 miles, then across the Tahoma Glacier or round Success Cleaver to the foot of the headwall.
text.overview: A steep, rimed headwall of snow and ice with short rock and ice steps at the head of the South Tahoma Glacier, dropping from Point Success. Slopes reach about 55 degrees, and an icy step high on the face has been rappelled by skiers. Rockfall and icefall are the main hazards.

text.approach: From Westside Road — Dry Creek Trailhead, walk the closed road past the barricade to the Tahoma Creek Trail and climb it about 2 miles to the Wonderland Trail junction near 4300 ft. Go south over the Tahoma Creek suspension bridge, follow the Wonderland Trail to Indian Henry's Hunting Ground, then take the Mirror Lakes Trail until it fades in the basin between Copper and Pyramid Peaks. Continue cross-country past Pyramid Peak to Success Cleaver and climb it to about 8000 ft, where glacier travel begins. A roped traverse across the South Tahoma Glacier at roughly 8100 ft reaches the base of Tahoma Cleaver.

text.overview: A rocky cleaver between the Tahoma Glacier and the South Tahoma Glacier on Rainier's southwest side, near 9,400 ft. Parties camp on it and use it as a climbing and ski line from the west side.

Approach via the Westside Road, Paradise, or Van Trump Meadows, then ascend the Success Couloir that lies farthest east, on snow of 45+ degrees. From Paradise or Van Trump the easiest line may be to cross the lower part of the Kautz Glacier and head up the Kautz Cleaver, then angle into the couloir. A lengthy snow ramp climbs nearly straight up. Rock bands may show near 12,600 feet and 13,300 depending on snow. text.approach: Drive to Ruth Creek Road's end at Hannegan Campground via Mt. Baker Hwy (SR 542) and Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32)/Ruth Creek Road. From the Ruth Creek trail at about 3,450 ft, leave the trail, drop southwest to cross Ruth Creek, and cross talus to the base of the couloir at about 4,000 ft.

text.overview: A confined snow/ice/rock couloir on Sefrit's north side (also called the North Couloir), climbing about 1,800 feet from talus above Ruth Creek to gain the upper snow slopes of Nooksack Ridge near the summit crest.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead (Trail #674, FR-32)
waypoints.directions: From Glacier, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR-542) east about 13 miles and turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FR-32). Follow it about 5.3 miles to its end at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead beside Hannegan Campground, at about 3,120 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and a free self-issue Mount Baker Wilderness permit is available at the trailhead.

waypoints.directions: Drop southwest to Ruth Creek and cross it (no bridge, no established log), then climb talus on the far side to the foot of the couloir at about 4,000 ft.

text.approach: Drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) to Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32); at 1.3 miles bear left onto Ruth Creek Road and continue to a pullout near milepost 3, just past a creek flowing over a concrete weir (about 2,950 ft), well short of the road's end at Hannegan Campground. From the pullout, cross Ruth Creek (a log crossing has been used) and bushwhack roughly 45 minutes through slide alder and devil's club to the base of the Wall Street couloir.

text.overview: The classic north-side line: a steep snow gully ('Wall Street') gains the Northwest Glacier, which is crossed to a 6,500-ft saddle west of the summit, followed by a Class 2-3 scramble up the exposed southeast ridge to the top.
text.descent: Reverse the southeast-ridge scramble to the 6,500-ft saddle, re-cross the Northwest Glacier, and plunge-step down the roughly 1,500-ft Wall Street couloir back to the bushwhack and Ruth Creek crossing.

name: First Divide Route (North Fork Skokomish / Staircase approach)

text.approach: From the Staircase trailhead area on the North Fork Skokomish River, follow the North Fork Skokomish River Trail 12.7 miles to First Divide (elevation about 4,688 ft), passing through lowland and montane forest into subalpine meadow with views of the La Crosse Peaks. From First Divide, continue cross-country to reach Mount Steel's summit. In August, the full day from Staircase to the summit and back is roughly 29 miles with around 7,000 ft of gain, so it is a very long single push or an overnight at the lower camps.

text.descent: Reverse the ascent: from the summit block follow the ridge south to the saddle between Steel's two summits, then work northeast around the north side of the small lake in the basin and back east along the ridge to First Divide. text.overview: Lichen and loose rock mar parts of this bigger outing, which adds roughly 1200 feet and sustained 5.9+ cracks to the regular North Ridge. Easy fifth class follows the crest above the hardest early pitches, which include a slot and a long layback crack past a small roof. Bivouac sites sit around 8200 feet at the notch. Time varies enormously: a rapid half-day simul-climbing, or several days if pitched out.

P2 (5.9): leftward through hanging corners and arete turns to a bolted ledge. P3 (5.10+): face holds to a 4 inch crack and a slung horn near big orange roofs, then diagonal cracks right; may be easier as two pitches. P4 (5.10-): finger cracks and stemming. text.approach: Reached via the longer, rougher Triumph Pass climbers' route rather than the standard Thornton Lakes approach used for the Northeast Ridge; used far less often and much less documented than the NE Ridge approach.
text.overview: The technically easiest way up Mount Triumph but the least climbed line: a long Class 4 route up the mountain's west side and south face to the southeast shoulder, reached via the much longer and rougher Triumph Pass climbers' route rather than the popular Thornton Lakes approach used for the Northeast Ridge.

text.approach: Start at the Jefferson Pass trailhead at the end of FR-2419, beside the Mount Washington trailhead, and follow the drainages west/toward the mountain, mixing bushwhacking with snow travel; parties have reported getting off-route on this approach.

text.overview: A winter/spring route up Mount Washington from Jefferson Pass: mostly trail-walking, bushwhacking, and snow travel, finishing with a single pitch of steep snow and chossy rock in a hidden gully below the summit.
text.descent: The winter descent is long and largely on snow; carry two 60m ropes to allow full-length double-rope rappels down the steepest slopes, supplemented by face-in downclimbing on lower-angle sections. In late February the steep, hard snow below the summit ridge called for a pair of rope rappels, using trees or snow anchors, before the angle eased.

text.approach: The standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of North Peak's granite West Face; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.

text.overview: The West Face of North Peak is one of the Cascades' sheerest and cleanest granite faces, offering world-class alpine rock climbing. The route ascends the center of the face with excellent crack and face climbing on solid white granite. Originally established as an aid route in 1986, the first free ascent in 2007 demonstrated the exceptional quality of the line, with sustained 5.11 climbing featuring hard crack work, bulbous knobs, lieback sections, and wild exposure.
text.descent: Rappel down the center of the West Face via four consecutive double-rope rappels of roughly 50 m, 50 m, 50 m and 20 m, using natural anchor features and existing bolt/gear anchors established on the granite. Ensure proper rope management to avoid tangling on the steep granite face. Once back at the base of the route, climb back up to the Chikamin-Dome Col via the Chickamin Glacier approach, watchi

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Darrington, drive SR 530 north about 8 miles to the Suiattle River Road (FS Road 26) and follow it east about 20 miles to the Downey Creek Trailhead at about 1,450 feet, just past the Downey Creek bridge; the trail leaves the north side of the road and parking is on the south side. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required. The Suiattle River Road has been closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 since the December 2025 flood washouts, which adds about 16 miles each way on foot or by bike, and the Downey Creek Trail has also been under a fire closure; check both before you go.

waypoints.name: Bachelor Flats (Camp 1)
waypoints.directions: Follow the Downey Creek Trail about 6.6 miles to its end at Bachelor Creek, cross the creek on a log, and follow the unmaintained Bachelor Creek path through heavy brush and slide alder about 3 miles up the valley to the flat camps at about 4,500 feet.

waypoints.name: Chikamin-Dome Col (Camp 2/High Camp)
waypoints.directions: From Bachelor Flats, continue up the path to the pass at about 5,900 feet and drop steeply to Cub Lake, then climb to Itswoot Ridge and follow it until the path fades at the snow. Traverse the Dome Glacier east to the col with the Chickamin Glacier at about 8,500 feet, where there are camps on both sides.

waypoints.name: North Peak Summit
waypoints.directions: From the col, make a descending traverse across the Chikamin Glacier, watching for crevasses and crossing the bergschrund on a snow bridge, to the foot of the West Face. Scramble along the ramp beneath the left side of the face to where it splits; the route starts just past the split at a small cairn. Climb five pitches to the terminal terrace, then move right along the terrace to a chimney that leads to the summit.
